questions.question_text: Choose the idiom that means "to be very expensive": ___.
options: hit the nail on the head
cost an arm and a leg

questions.question_text: The idiom "spill the beans" means to:
The idiom "break the ice" means to:
options: Reveal a secret that others have been keeping
End a long-standing argument between two parties
Ease the tension at the start of a meeting
Cancel an event because of the cold weather

questions.question_text: The idiom "hit the nail on the head" means to:
options: Describe exactly what is causing a situation
Strike the central point of a quarrel angrily
Complete a long task in a hurry
Make a mistake through careless work

questions.question_text: The idiom "the ball is in your court" means that:
options: You have been blamed for a failure
You must wait for the others to decide
You have gained the upper hand in an argument
It is your turn to take the next step

questions.question_text: The idiom "burn the midnight oil" means to:
options: Start a business project in the dark hours
Cause a fire through careless behaviour
Work or study late into the night

questions.question_text: The idiom "a blessing in disguise" means:
options: A misfortune that follows a period of good luck
A favour that is done secretly without credit
Something that seems bad but turns out to be good
A good wish from a stranger met in a crowd

questions.question_text: The idiom "bite the bullet" means to:
options: Speak harshly to a colleague at a meeting
Face an unpleasant situation with courage
Take a very big risk with someone's money
Refuse to take part in a difficult task

The idiom "a piece of cake" means something that is:
The idiom "cut corners" means to:
options: Follow the rules strictly at every step of the work
Reduce the number of employees in a department
Do something cheaply or carelessly to save time or money
Take the shortest route to reach the office early

questions.question_text: The idiom "on the same page" means:
options: Reading the same report at the same time
Sharing the same understanding or agreement
Sitting together at the same table in a meeting
Working at the same pace as the other team members

questions.question_text: The idiom "back to the drawing board" means:
The idiom "touch base" means to:
The idiom "think outside the box" means to:
options: Think creatively and in an unconventional way
Think about the matters outside the office premises
Avoid thinking about the matters in detail
Think quickly without consulting anyone else

tests.title: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: Select the one-word substitute for "a person who speaks many languages".
Select the one-word substitute for "able to use both hands equally well".
Select the one-word substitute for "government by the wealthy".
Select the one-word substitute for "a person who doubts that God's existence can be known".
Select the one-word substitute for "a place where bees are kept".
Select the one-word substitute for "the study of ancient societies through their remains".
Select the one-word substitute for "a speech delivered without preparation".
Select the one-word substitute for "an irrational fear of closed spaces".
Select the one-word substitute for "one who takes a gloomy view of every situation".
Select the one-word substitute for "a speech by a character alone on the stage".
Choose the correct collocation: "She ___ a decision after a long discussion."
Choose the correct collocation: "The company has decided to ___ a loan from the bank."
Choose the correct collocation: "He was ___ with a heavy fine for the offence."
Choose the correct collocation: "The manager ___ a meeting to discuss the sales."
Choose the correct collocation: "They finally ___ a deal after three weeks of talks."
Which is the correct way to write a line of dialogue in a story?
options: I will be there by noon, said Rahul.
"I will be there by noon", said Rahul.
"I will be there by noon," said Rahul.
"I will be there by noon" said Rahul.

questions.question_text: In writing dialogue, a new paragraph should begin when:
Which dialogue tag shows anger?
options: "Get out of my office!" he shouted.

questions.question_text: In dialogue writing, stage directions or actions are usually given in:
A natural-sounding dialogue should:
options: Avoid contractions and everyday expressions throughout
Contain no pauses or hesitations at any point
Reflect real speech, including short sentences and interruptions
Use long formal sentences in all the speakers' turns

questions.question_text: When writing a dialogue for a business meeting between a manager and an employee, the tone should be:
Which is the best opening for a telephone call to a customer?
options: Hey, what do you want? Make it quick, please.
Good morning, this is Priya from Sunrise Traders. How may I help you?
Yeah, who is this and what do you want to say right now?
Hello, hello? Please say something quickly as I am busy.

questions.question_text: To politely ask a caller to wait, you should say:
options: Do not hang up, or you will lose the line again.
Please wait, and do not call again till I call you.
Hold on, I am busy at the moment with some work.
Could you please hold the line for a moment?

questions.question_text: To politely disagree in a meeting, you might say:
options: You are wrong, and the data does not support you.
That is a poor idea and we should drop it now.
I see your point, but I have a slightly different view.
I refuse to listen to the proposal any further.

questions.question_text: To politely ask a colleague to repeat something, you might say:
options: You are not clear at all.
Sorry, could you repeat that, please?

tests.title: Unit 4: Speaking Skills: Vocabulary, Dialogue Writing and Storytelling – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: The five basic elements of a story are:
options: Introduction, thesis, body, evidence and conclusion
Verbs, nouns, adjectives, adverbs and articles
Title, author, price, pages and cover
Characters, setting, plot, conflict and resolution

questions.question_text: The setting of a story refers to:
options: The central problem that the character faces
The main character who drives the events
The time and place in which the events happen
The final outcome that ends the events

questions.question_text: The climax of a story is:
options: The title that is chosen by the author for the story
The closing line that gives the moral of the story
The turning point where the tension is at its highest
The opening scene that introduces the characters

questions.question_text: The conflict in a story is:
options: The place and time in which the story is set
The name given by the author to the story
The central problem or struggle faced by the characters
The lesson that the story leaves with the reader

questions.question_text: The "resolution" of a story is where:
options: The conflict is resolved and the story ends

questions.question_text: A story told from the point of view of "I" is told in the:
A story told with "he", "she" and "they" is in the:
In a good story opening, a writer should:
options: Describe all the characters at length
Capture the reader's interest at once

questions.question_text: A flashback in a story is:
options: A scene that repeats the ending at the beginning
A scene that jumps ahead to an event in the future
A scene that returns to an event from an earlier time
A scene that describes a dream of the character

questions.question_text: "Foreshadowing" in a story is:
options: A hint of what will happen later

questions.question_text: Business storytelling is used to:
options: Make a message memorable and persuasive
Replace the facts and the data

questions.question_text: A good business story usually includes:
options: A relatable character, a challenge and an outcome
A quotation from a famous person and nothing else
A long list of statistics with no people in it
A joke at the start with no link to the point

questions.question_text: The "STAR" method of telling an experience in an interview stands for:
In an interview, a story about solving a problem under pressure shows your:
options: Skills and experience through a real example
Age and the number of years you spent in school
Family background and the place where you grew up
Weaknesses that you want the interviewer to know

questions.question_text: The best way to open a speech is to:
options: Read the whole speech from the paper
Thank the audience for ten minutes
Use a surprising fact, a question or a short story

questions.question_text: Eye contact while speaking helps to:
options: Build trust and engage the audience
Hide nervousness by looking at the floor

questions.question_text: When speaking to a large audience, the pace should be:
options: Continuous, with no pause between the sentences
As fast as possible, to save the time of the audience
Very slow throughout, to be understood by all

questions.question_text: The stress in "PREsent" (noun) and "preSENT" (verb) shows that:
options: Verbs are never stressed in the spoken English
Stress has no effect on the meaning of a word
Stress can change the meaning and the part of speech
Both the words are stressed on the same syllable

questions.question_text: Which sentence has the correct intonation for a question that expects "yes" or "no"?
options: Rising intonation at the end: "Are you coming?"
Falling intonation: "Are you coming?" in all cases
Falling intonation: "Are you coming?" for yes-no questions

questions.question_text: To appear confident in a presentation, a speaker should:
options: Stand straight, speak clearly and use natural gestures
Fold the arms and avoid looking at the audience
Look at the floor and speak in a low voice
Speak very fast to finish before the audience tires

questions.question_text: Filler words such as "um" and "you know" can be reduced by:
options: Using them at the end of each sentence
Repeating them for emphasis at the end of a point
Using them often so as to sound natural

questions.question_text: "Active listening" in a conversation involves:
options: Paying full attention, nodding and giving feedback
Planning your reply while the other speaks

questions.question_text: To keep a conversation going, you can use:
An elevator pitch is:
options: A written report of about ten pages for the management
A short persuasive summary of an idea given in under a minute
A long speech given to a large audience in a lift lobby
A sales brochure with photographs of the products

questions.question_text: A suitable closing for a presentation is to:
options: Summarise the key points and end with a clear call to action
Apologise to the audience for the time taken by the talk
Introduce a new topic that was not discussed before
Stop abruptly after the last slide without any remark
